question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2
solution:
The correct answer is '**Connecting**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The passage discusses John Biggins' invention of the 'Charge-It' program, which connected bank customers and local merchants.
 
• "**Connecting**" is the correct word, as it implies linking two parties, which in this case refers to the relationship between bank customers and merchants through the credit card system.
 
• Other options ("untangling," "smashing," "splitting") are inappropriate. "Untangling" refers to resolving confusion or mess, "smashing" suggests forceful breaking, and "splitting" implies dividing, none of which align with the context of establishing a connection.

Therefore, the correct answer is '**Option 2**'.

 

Complete Passage: *Credit cards originated in the 1920s in the US, with European references dating back to 1890. John Biggins, inventor__ of the first bank-issued credit card, invented the 'Charge-It' programme in 1946, __connecting__ bank customers and local merchants. In 1950, Diners Club introduced their credit card in the US, __allowing__ customers to pay restaurant bills without cash. American Express __launched__ their first credit card in 1958, while the Bank of America introduced the Bank America Card (now Visa) in 1958. Visa, now known as the Visa International Service Association, is accepted in over 150 countries, making it one of the most __widely used__ credit cards available.*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• "Untangling" refers to resolving something complicated, which is not the intended meaning in the context of connecting parties.
 
• "Smashing" means forcefully breaking something, which is not appropriate here as it has no relevance to the connection of customers and merchants.
 
• "Splitting" suggests dividing or separating, which contradicts the idea of connecting bank customers and merchants.
